comments.note: NameParser.cs: the date pattern regex uses a character class [.\-] for the separator. The escaped hyphen needs to be at the start or end of a character class to avoid ambiguity. Currently written as [.\-] which is correct (escaped hyphen), but [.-] could be misread as a range in some regex engines. The current form is safe in .NET but a comment noting the intent would aid future maintainers.

NameParser.AssembleLabel: trailing tokens after the last separator are discarded (ported from legacy behaviour). This is a documented limitation but could silently drop content if a filename ends with a bracket-delimited section followed by more text. If the label assembly ever produces unexpectedly short results, this is the first place to investigate.

LabelCleanerOptions.Keywords is typed as IReadOnlyList<string> with an empty collection default. Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration binds JSON arrays to IReadOnlyList<string> in .NET 10 without issue, but if a downstream caller mutates the list via reflection or unsafe casting the defaults become corrupted. The record sealed type makes this unlikely but worth noting.

summary: All 8 acceptance criteria verified for NameParser / LabelCleaner WP.

AC2: Three DatePatterns (yyyymmdd/ddmmyyyy/yymmdd) verified; PreserveDates flag tested on/off.

comments.note: GetFullWordMatches in NameParser.cs uses three patterns that all require at least one space bounding the actor name ('\A(term)[ ]', '[ ](term)\z', '[ ](term)[ ]'). If the remaining text after studio/date extraction is exactly the actor name with no surrounding tokens, no match occurs. Example: filename 'Jane.Doe' (after normalization 'Jane Doe') with knownActorNames=["Jane Doe"] — actor is not detected. Low probability in practice (filenames normally include title tokens), but the gap is untest-covered.

yymmdd date normalisation produces dd-mm-yyyy output (e.g. '16.12.30' → '30-12-2016') per legacy app behaviour. The Format label 'yymmdd' is slightly misleading since the tokens map yy→century, mm, dd. Covered by test and documented in comment; no functional issue.

INameParser is registered as singleton in Program.cs (line 159) which is correct per the interface docs. Verified no mutable state in NameParser — all methods are static helpers called from the single Parse method.

summary: Reviewed 8 files. 0 Critical, 0 High, 0 Medium, 2 Low, 1 Info. Security sign-off: PASS. All OWASP Top 10 categories reviewed. Regex injection risk is mitigated by consistent use of Regex.Escape on all caller-supplied terms. No secrets, no external network calls, no auth surfaces in the modified code.

comments.note: A03 — Injection (Low/Info): NameParser.cs — GetFullWordMatches and GetSubstringMatches both call Regex.Escape on the caller-supplied term before building the regex pattern, eliminating regex injection. DetectStudios also uses Regex.Escape. All date patterns are static readonly constants. No injection vectors identified.

A03 — ReDoS (Low): NameParser.GetFullWordMatches — the alternation pattern duplicates the escaped term three times (start-of-string, end-of-string, surrounded-by-spaces). Inputs come from the internal database (knownActorNames/knownStudios), not raw external user input. No complex nested quantifiers are present. ReDoS risk is low but could be reduced further by pre-compiling these regexes as static readonly fields (also a performance improvement).

A03 — Regex instantiation in hot path (Low): ExtractDates instantiates new Regex objects on every Parse call for each of the 3 DatePatterns. The patterns are static constants; pre-compiling them as static readonly Regex fields (with RegexOptions.Compiled) would eliminate per-call allocation and any theoretical risk from repeated construction. Not a security vulnerability but worth addressing alongside the GetFullWordMatches note above.

A08 — Data Integrity (Info/Positive): appsettings.json FFmpeg provisioning block includes SHA256 hashes for all download targets (win-x64, win-arm64, linux-x64). This is a sound integrity control that should be validated at download time. Confirm the provisioning code verifies the hash before extracting the archive.

summary: Reviewed 8 implementation files. Architecture is sound — INameParser/LabelCleanerResult/LabelCleanerOptions correctly reside in Core with no NuGet dependencies; NameParser lives in Infrastructure and is registered as a singleton. DI registration in Program.cs is correct.

Applied Fix-Forward: pre-compiled the three static date regex patterns as `static readonly (Regex CompiledRegex, string Format)[]` entries with RegexOptions.Compiled, eliminating per-call Regex allocation flagged by the Security Auditor. Build and all 537 tests verified green.

No blocking issues found. One low-priority inconsistency noted between DetectStudios (removes all occurrences) and DetectActorNames (only removes the first occurrence of a repeated actor name). Real-world impact is negligible — actor names rarely repeat in a filename — and does not block approval.
AssembleLabel trailing-token discard is documented in code and faithfully ports legacy behaviour. The debt comment from the Developer is sufficient.

comments.note: NameParser.cs — Pre-compiled the three static date regex patterns. Changed `static readonly (string Pattern, string Format)[]` to `static readonly (Regex CompiledRegex, string Format)[]` with `RegexOptions.IgnoreCase | RegexOptions.Compiled`. Updated `ExtractDates` to destructure `(regex, format)` directly rather than constructing a new `Regex` per call. Addresses the Security Auditor's low-priority ReDoS/allocation recommendation. Non-behavioral change — all 537 tests pass.

NameParser.DetectActorNames — Minor inconsistency with DetectStudios: the text replacement is guarded by `!detected.Contains(name)`, so if the same actor name appears multiple times in the post-processing text, only the first occurrence is removed. DetectStudios removes all occurrences unconditionally before adding to `detected`. Real-world impact is negligible (actor names rarely repeat in a single filename); flagging for awareness. Not blocking.

[documentation-forward] INameParser.Parse — the XML doc comment on the `knownActorNames` parameter should note the full-word matching boundary requirement: an actor name that equals the entire remaining text (no surrounding tokens) will not be detected by GetFullWordMatches. This is a known gap (flagged by QA, AC3 does not require exhaustive matching) but should be surfaced to consumers of the API surface so they understand the edge case.

LabelCleanerTests.cs — No test exercises the DetectStudios vs. DetectActorNames removal-consistency difference noted above. If the inconsistency is ever fixed a regression test for 'actor name repeated in filename' would lock in the behaviour.
